title: continuous-batching-scheduler-draft-v5
content:
Purpose
This is a working draft for the Continuous Batching Scheduler used by the serving runtime. It compares token-level vs request-level batching designs, explores fairness across tenants and priority classes, and highlights interactions with KV cache and kernel selection.

Context & motivation
- We need predictable low p50/p95 latency for interactive use cases while maintaining high GPU throughput for bursty workloads.
- Current request-level micro-batching (pack whole requests until max_batch or timeout) is simple but struggles with streaming workloads and long-sequence tails.
- Token-level scheduling can improve head-of-line latency for streaming and mixed-length workloads but adds complexity (preemption, KV cache ownership, kernel lifecycle).

Requirements / constraints
- Latency SLOs: target p50 < 40ms and p95 < 250ms for interactive tier, with hard SLA degrade thresholds.
- Throughput objective: maximize GPU utilization and tokens/sec for batch workloads without violating latency SLOs.
- Memory constraint: limited KV cache memory per GPU; must avoid uncontrolled KV growth.
- Fairness: multi-tenant fairness across customers + per-customer fairness across routes/priorities. No tenant starvation.
- Kernel compatibility: some kernels require uniform sequence lengths or specific packing patterns; scheduling must expose compatible batches to kernel selector.

Design alternatives
1) Request-level batching (baseline)
   - Behavior: accumulate whole requests into a batch and execute once a batch is full or timeout reached.
   - Pros: simple, easier KV/cache accounting (request owns KV during execution), kernel-friendly (uniform control), minimal preemption logic.
   - Cons: long requests delay short interactive ones; streaming requires buffering full requests or breaking request in app code; poor utilization with highly variable seq lengths.

2) Token-level batching (proposed hybrid)
   - Behavior: schedule work per token step. Each in-flight request contributes tokens to a shared token queue. Scheduler forms batches of tokens from different requests and advances their KV cache accordingly.
   - Pros: better interactivity (short requests get scheduled quickly), improved latency tail for streaming, better packing across seq-lengths, potentially higher GPU throughput.
   - Cons: complex: preemption, KV cache sharding and ownership, partial-kernel execution, more kernel variants needed, harder debugging.

Key tradeoffs
- Latency vs Throughput: token-level favors lower tail latency but may add kernel overheads and more kernel launches per request. Request-level favors throughput but increases queuing latency for short requests.
- Fairness vs Efficiency: strict fairness (e.g., round-robin tokens) can reduce packing efficiency; batching similar-length tokens increases utilization but risks starvation.
- KV cache semantics: token-level requires per-request KV state to be addressable and possibly locked per-step; request-level can lock KV per full request execute.

Scheduling primitives and algorithms
- Admission controller: decide whether a new request is accepted or queued based on tenant quotas, per-route priorities, and current backlog. Reject or reroute when overloaded.
- Token queue: a central structure holding (request_id, priority, next_position, seq_len_remaining, kv_handle). Implemented as multiple logical queues keyed by priority class.
- Batch builder: forms batches of tokens each GPU step. Options:
    * Round-robin token selection: pick up to N tokens across tenants in round-robin order (fairness-friendly).
    * Weighted fair token scheduling: allocate tokens proportionally to tenant weight (for paid tiers).
    * Packing-first selection: pick tokens that lead to homogeneous sequence lengths for kernel compatibility (efficiency-first).
- Watermarks and deadlines: each request gets a soft token-level deadline (absolute or relative to arrival) to prevent indefinite deferral. If deadline approaches, escalate priority or preempt other tokens.
- Preemption and yield: implement cooperative preemption where long-running kernel executions yield on slice boundaries. Use micro-batching to bound execution time per chunk (e.g., max 8 tokens per slice).

KV cache considerations
- KV ownership: keep per-request KV metadata (kv_handle) in CPU-side metadata store and map to GPU cache shards. Token-level scheduling must be able to fetch and attach the KV cache pointers quickly.
- Cache warmup: if a request’s KV is not resident, fetching it incurs latency. Scheduler should prioritize cached KVs for low-latency responses and use background prefetch for hot tenants.
- Partial KV updates: because token-level advances KV incrementally, we must ensure atomic updates to KV indices or use per-request KV slices to avoid corruption.
- Memory accounting: enforce per-tenant KV memory caps and eviction policy (LRU with tenant-weight adjustments).

Kernel & runtime interactions
- Kernel selector: scheduler must provide kernel-compatible batches (sequence length distribution, quantization type, and attention masks). Extend kernel metadata to include 'batching-friendliness' score.
- Multi-kernel pipeline: when batches contain mixed types, we may either transform inputs (pad/pack) or split batches into kernel-homogeneous sub-batches. Splitting reduces latency benefits of token-level scheduling.
- Kernel launch overhead: token-level scheduling increases number of kernel launches. Mitigate with micro-batching (group multiple tokens into a single kernel run when possible) and fused kernels for streaming steps.

Fairness policies and enforcement
- Per-tenant quotas: enforce token-rate limits and max concurrent tokens. Exceeding quota triggers queuing or throttling.
- Priority classes: each request has priority (interactive, background, batch) which maps to scheduling weights and deadline policies.
- Elastic weights: allow dynamic weight adjustments based on recent SLA violations or customer-configured priorities.
- Starvation protection: implement minimum throughput guarantees: within any window T, each active tenant must receive min_tokens proportional to min_weight.

Operational metrics to expose
- Scheduling: tokens_waiting, tokens_scheduled_per_sec, avg_token_queue_time, p50/p95 token_schedule_latency.
- KV cache: kv_hit_rate, kv_fetch_latency, kv_evictions_per_sec, kv_memory_by_tenant.
- Kernel: kernel_utilization, kernel_launches_per_sec, average_batch_size_tokens, packing_efficiency.
- Fairness: tokens_by_tenant_window, missed_deadlines_by_tenant.

Experiments & rollout plan
- Phase 0: simulation harness (offline) that replays production traces and compares request-level vs token-level scheduling under different mixes. Metrics: p50/p95 latencies, GPU tokens/sec, KV hit-rate, fairness violation rate.
- Phase 1: implement token-queue + admission controller + batch builder behind feature flag. Run canary on low-risk test cluster with synthetic workloads.
- Phase 2: hybrid mode for interactive tier only (token-level) and batch tier remains request-level. Collect telemetry for 2 weeks.
- Phase 3: full rollout with dynamic mode selection based on route and SLOs.

Open questions / TODOs
- Kernel API changes required to support partial-step execution and fast switching between requests. (TODO: draft kernel interface by 2024-12-10)
- How to minimize KV fetch latency for cold requests in token-level mode? Options: shallow prefetch, piggyback KV fetch on admission, or accept slight latency spike. Need benchmarks.
- Preemption strategy: implement cooperative preemption first, evaluate need for hardware/driver-level preemption.
- Packing heuristics: experiment with greedy vs lookahead packers to balance packing efficiency and fairness.
- Load-shedding policy: define clear behavior for admitted but throttled requests when overloaded.

Implementation notes / low-level details
- Data structures: use lock-free per-priority ring buffers for token queues to reduce contention. Maintain a fast bitmap of resident KV shards for quick cache hit checks.
- Time-slicing: define a scheduling epoch (e.g., 4ms) where a batch is formed and dispatched to GPU. Tune epoch based on observed kernel latency and queue dynamics.
- Accounting: maintain per-request deadline and per-tenant token counters in shared atomic counters to simplify fairness checks.
- Failures: ensure requests can be replayed if partially executed slices fail; store minimal idempotency markers.

References / related docs
- continuous-batching-scheduler-draft.json (v1..v4) — earlier drafts with simulation traces.
- PR-842 — kernel selector changes for batching.
- JIRA SRV-378 — KV cache memory accounting work.

Action items
- [Maya] prototype token-queue + simple round-robin token selection (2 weeks).
- [Liam] benchmark KV fetch patterns and produce cold-hit latency curves (1 week).
- [Ava] extend kernel metadata for batching-friendliness and propose selector heuristics (2 weeks).
- [All] align on metrics and dashboard for canary.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally high-level and pragmatic. Looking for feedback on fairness goals, KV semantics, and rollout sequencing. Please leave comments inline or ping in #serving-runtime.
